loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 1 of 6 · Prerequisites — "The three CSI requirements", the version-context paragraph
orig: Read the first two against the release you are actually running. The Storage Integration page states the baseline as Kubernetes v1.14.0 with the VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature enabled [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102], while the versions Veeam Kasten 9.0.2 supports begin at Kubernetes 1.29 [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862] — every supported release is far past that baseline, so treat those two lines as inherited history rather than work on your list. The third requirement is the one that still has to be proved on your cluster, and Section 2 is how you prove it.
prop: Read the first two against the release you are actually running. The Storage Integration page states the baseline as Kubernetes v1.14.0 with the VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature enabled [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102], while the support matrix for this build runs from Kubernetes 1.31 to 1.34 on any certified distribution, with 1.30 and 1.29 supported only when the cluster is deployed as OpenShift 4.17 or 4.16 [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862] — every one of those releases is far past that baseline, so treat those two lines as inherited history rather than work on your list. Check your own version against that matrix before anything else in this section: a vanilla Kubernetes 1.30 cluster is not a supported target, however clean its pre-flight run comes back. The third requirement is the one that still has to be proved on your cluster, and Section 2 is how you prove it.
why: Misstates the supported floor for vanilla Kubernetes, and Module 04 already contradicts it. The matrix on Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862 lists 1.34/4.21 down to 1.29/4.16, and annotates both 1.30/4.17 and 1.29/4.16 with "Kubernetes version *only* supported when deployed as an OpenShift cluster" — so on a certified non-OpenShift distribution the supported range starts at 1.31, not 1.29. The 8.5.9 release notes say the same thing from the other direction: "Removed support for Kubernetes 1.30. OpenShift 4.17 clusters continue to be supported" (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1099). Module 04's own matrix reproduces the OpenShift-only caveat on both rows, so as it stands the course tells a platform team two different things about the same page. In the field this is the row that decides whether a support case gets opened or closed: a team on EKS or Rancher at 1.30 reads "1.29 and later", installs, and finds out the release is out of the matrix at the worst possible moment.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 2 of 6 · Deployment-readiness checklist, blocking item 3 (rdy2)
why: Same error as KA-v3-001, in the place where it does the most damage — a blocking checklist item a team ticks to decide whether to open the install window. "Every release this build supports — Kubernetes 1.29 and later" invites a team on vanilla 1.29 or 1.30 to tick a blocking gate they do not actually pass; the matrix marks both of those rows "Kubernetes version *only* supported when deployed as an OpenShift cluster" (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862). The rewrite also fixes what the item is really gating: the checkbox should be about matching the matrix, not about a feature gate that no longer exists on any supported release. The primer's Kubernetes Version Check reports the version (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.871) but nothing in the tool tells you the OpenShift-only caveat, so this has to be read by a human off the matrix.

prop: The annotation is what matters; the API group has moved on. The guide also illustrates this object with its Alpha and Beta snapshot API examples [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102, p.103], but on every Kubernetes release in this build's support matrix — 1.31 to 1.34, and 1.30 or 1.29 only as OpenShift [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862] — the group is snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1, as shown here. why: Third and last instance of the "1.29 and later" shorthand (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862 marks 1.29 and 1.30 as OpenShift-only). Graded minor rather than significant because the argument the sentence is making — use the v1 API group, not the beta one — is correct on every release in the matrix either way, so no learner is mis-led about the manifest. It is fixed here only so the course states the matrix the same way in all three places it appears.

loc: Lesson05_Restores_and_Day_to_Day_Administration.html · Who can do what · 04 — the four roles table, k10-basic row, "What it allows" cell (shipped [VERIFY] marker)
orig: Operational access in specific namespaces. Within assigned namespaces the holder may manually back up and restore applications, create and modify policies, view application, action and restore point details, and cancel actions [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.272]. That documented capability list stops there — it does not name deletion — while the published ClusterRole definition grants all verbs on the policies and restorepoints resources in the namespaces the role is bound to [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.274]. [VERIFY: whether a k10-basic holder can delete a restore point or a policy, or whether deletion is effectively reserved to k10-admin — the capability list and the role definition point different ways, so confirm it on your own cluster before you answer "who can delete our backups" from this table.]
prop: Operational access in specific namespaces. Within assigned namespaces the holder may manually back up and restore applications, create and modify policies, view application, action and restore point details, and cancel actions [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.272]. Read that list as a summary, not as a limit — and read the role definition when the question is "who can delete our backups". Veeam Kasten leverages Kubernetes ClusterRoles and Bindings for role-based access [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.264], so what the ClusterRole grants is what the holder can do: the published k10-basic ClusterRole carries verbs: '*' on the action resources, on restorepoints and applications, on policies, and on filerecoverysessions [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.273, p.274]. All verbs includes delete. So in every namespace you bind this role into, the holder can delete restore points and policies as well as create them. That is the blast radius of a tenant grant — size it before you hand out the RoleBinding, and if you need protection from deletion, put it in an immutable export location profile rather than in the role.
why: RESOLVES the shipped [VERIFY]. This is not a documentation self-contradiction — it is an incomplete prose summary sitting next to a normative role definition, and the guide tells you which one governs. Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.264: "For facilitating role-based access for users, Veeam Kasten leverages Kubernetes ClusterRoles and Bindings." Authorization is therefore Kubernetes RBAC, and the published k10-basic ClusterRole (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.273–274) grants verbs: '*' on backupactions/restoreactions/exportactions/cancelactions/runactions and their /details subresources, on restorepoints and applications, on policies, and on filerecoverysessions, plus get on namespaces. '*' includes delete. The capability list on p.272 simply does not enumerate deletion; it never claims to be exhaustive, and nothing anywhere in the guide says a k10-basic holder is denied deletion. Leaving a [VERIFY] on the answer to "who can delete our backups" is worse than the answer itself — the answer is citable, it is the alarming one, and a platform team designing multi-tenancy needs it before they bind the role, not after their first "where did that restore point go" conversation. Two field notes I have deliberately kept out of the proposed text because the 9.0.2 guide does not state them: the dashboard may not surface a delete control for every one of those objects, and an 8.5.x release note records that "Basic users now require specific permission to view each action type through the Veeam Kasten dashboard" (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1111) — so UI reachability and API authorization are not the same surface. Recommend SME confirmation on the UI half; the RBAC half needs none.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 3 of 6 · "Before you tear it down" callout, second paragraph (shipped [VERIFY] marker)
orig: The 9.0.2 guide does not publish a retry procedure for a partially completed install [VERIFY: whether the kasten-io namespace and the catalog persistent volume claim must be removed before re-running helm install after a failed install — not addressed anywhere in the 9.0.2 guide; Architect to confirm before a learner is told it is safe]. Until that is confirmed, treat a stuck install as a support case with logs attached rather than a loop of retries.
prop: The 9.0.2 guide publishes no retry procedure for a partially completed install, but it does publish what to do when you reinstall on a cluster that has had Veeam Kasten on it before, and it is not "just run the command again". When reinstalling Veeam Kasten on the same cluster, it is important to clean up the namespace in which Veeam Kasten was previously installed, with kubectl delete namespace kasten-io [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.605]; the disaster-recovery workflow states the same step first — "Reinstall Veeam Kasten, deleting the Veeam Kasten namespace if reinstalling on the same cluster" [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.503]. Read that alongside the paragraph above and the order falls out: helm uninstall k10 --namespace=kasten-io first, because that is what clears the non-namespaced resources [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.865], then remove the namespace if it survives, then install again. [VERIFY: whether a straight helm install re-run without that cleanup is safe after a failed install specifically — the 9.0.2 guide addresses reinstallation but never the failed-install case, so the cleanup sequence above is the documented path and a bare retry is not; Kasten SME to confirm.] Until that is confirmed, do not loop retries: collect the debug bundle, do the documented cleanup, and install once more — or open a support case with the logs attached.
why: PARTIALLY RESOLVES the shipped [VERIFY], and the part it resolves matters more than the part it does not. The marker as shipped says the guide is silent, and that is too strong: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.605 carries an explicit Note — "When reinstalling Veeam Kasten on the same cluster, it is important to clean up the namespace in which Veeam Kasten was previously installed" — with the literal command, and the DR runbook on p.503 opens with the same instruction. Combined with the uninstall page (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.865: uninstall with Helm so non-namespaced resources are cleaned up; simply deleting the namespace "might cause issues with stale services"), the guide does yield a documented sequence, and that sequence is the answer to the question a learner is actually holding at 21:40. What is genuinely undocumented is narrower: whether a bare re-run is safe after a *failed* install. Keeping a marker on that narrower question is correct; keeping it on the whole subject leaves a learner with no procedure at all, which in practice means they will improvise the worst one — kubectl delete namespace with the Helm release still registered.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 6 of 6 · "Five things to know before you choose this route", first list item
orig: • Exporting to a Veeam Repository requires the use of the Block Mode Export mechanism for all volume snapshots created by the policy, and when a Veeam Repository is selected as the Export Location Profile, block mode export is enabled automatically [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.128].
prop: • Exporting to a Veeam Repository requires the use of the Block Mode Export mechanism for all volume snapshots created by the policy, and when a Veeam Repository is selected as the Export Location Profile, block mode export is enabled automatically [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.128]. Check that your provisioner can do it before you build the profile: a Veeam Repository is a destination for both application metadata and persistent volume snapshot data on any cluster where the storage provisioner for persistent volumes supports block mode export [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.127], and while both Filesystem and Block persistent volume modes are supported, only storage provisioners capable of performing block mode exports are compatible [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]. This is the go/no-go gate on the whole route, and it is a property of the CSI driver rather than something a Helm flag can add.
why: This section is the runbook page for creating a Veeam Repository location profile, and it never states the prerequisite that decides whether the route is available at all. The guide is explicit twice: the Veeam Repository destination applies to "any cluster where a Veeam Backup & Replication (VBR) repository is available, and the storage provisioner for persistent volumes supports block mode export" (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.127), and among the Considerations, "Both Filesystem and Block persistent volume modes are supported, however only storage provisioners capable of performing block mode exports are compatible" (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129). Module 01 carries this correctly, but Module 01 is the concept map and Module 03 is the page open on the second screen while someone fills in the dialog. The field failure is specific and common: the profile validates — it only checks reachability and credentials to the backup server — the policy saves, and then every export action fails on a provisioner that cannot do block mode. Naming the requirement here costs two sentences and moves the discovery from the first backup window to the design conversation.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 6 of 6 · "Immutability is a toggle, and it belongs on by default" paragraph
orig: Immutability is a toggle, and it belongs on by default. If the bucket has object locking enabled, set the Enable Immutable Backups toggle [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315] — this is the setting that protects exported restore points from tampering: in a locked bucket, restore point data cannot be deleted or modified within the set protection period, even with administrator privileges, so a clean copy survives an attacker who has obtained privileged object store credentials [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.341]. Module 04 gives this weight for the profile behind Veeam Kasten's own disaster recovery, and the control is the same one here: treat it as the standing choice for every production export location profile, not a special case. A profile without it is the first thing an auditor or a CISO will pick out of your configuration, and the answer “the bucket was not locked” is a procurement decision you want on the record before the review, not during it.
prop: Immutability is a toggle, and it belongs on by default. If the bucket has object locking enabled, set the Enable Immutable Backups toggle [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315] — this is the setting that protects exported restore points from tampering: in a locked bucket, restore point data cannot be deleted or modified within the set protection period, even with administrator privileges, so a clean copy survives an attacker who has obtained privileged object store credentials [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.341]. Module 04 gives this weight for the profile behind Veeam Kasten's own disaster recovery, and the control is the same one here: treat it as the standing choice for every production export location profile, not a special case. One documented exception, so you do not pay for nothing: the generic storage and shareable volume backup and restore workflows are not compatible with the protections immutable backups afford — such a profile still works, but the protection period is ignored and the profile is treated as non-immutable, and using an object-locking bucket for those workflows can amplify storage usage without any additional benefit [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.341]. A profile without immutability is the first thing an auditor or a CISO will pick out of your configuration, and the answer “the bucket was not locked” is a procurement decision you want on the record before the review, not during it.
why: "Standing choice for every production export location profile" is the right instruction for the common case and wrong for one documented case, and the guide flags it as a warning rather than a footnote: "The generic storage and shareable volume backup and restore workflows are not compatible with the protections afforded by immutable backups. Use of a location profile enabled for immutable backups can be used for backup and restore, but the protection period is ignored, and the profile is treated as a non-immutability-enabled location … using an object-locking bucket for such use cases can amplify storage usage without any additional benefit" (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.341). Minor, because Generic Storage Backup is a path the course already tells the reader to avoid (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090) — but the clusters that end up on GSB are exactly the ones without a snapshot-capable CSI driver, i.e. the ones a VDP administrator inherits, and "we enabled immutability everywhere" plus a surprise object-storage bill is a conversation worth pre-empting in one sentence.

loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · Concept · 06 · VolumeSnapshots — the three CSI requirements paragraph
orig: Veeam Kasten can invoke volume snapshot operations through CSI, and three requirements have to be met for that to work: Kubernetes v1.14.0 or higher, the VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature enabled in the cluster, and a CSI driver that has Volume Snapshot support [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]. Using a CSI driver with VolumeSnapshot support is described as a requirement for building a good data protection solution with Veeam Kasten [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090].
prop: Veeam Kasten can invoke volume snapshot operations through CSI, and three requirements have to be met for that to work: Kubernetes v1.14.0 or higher, the VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature enabled in the cluster, and a CSI driver that has Volume Snapshot support [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]. Read the first two as inherited history: the releases this build supports start at Kubernetes 1.31 on a certified distribution, with 1.30 and 1.29 supported only as OpenShift [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862], and volume snapshots became a stable API long before any of them — so there is no feature gate left for you to switch on. Only the third requirement still has to be proved on your cluster. Using a CSI driver with VolumeSnapshot support is described as a requirement for building a good data protection solution with Veeam Kasten [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090].
why: Accurate quotation, and this is the first place a learner meets it — without the version context that Module 03 supplies later. Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102 does state the v1.14.0 floor and the VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature gate, but the supported matrix (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862) starts far past both, and the gate does not exist to be enabled on any release in it. Module 03 fixes this in its own prerequisites section; Module 02 is where the concept lands first, and an admin who takes "three requirements have to be met" literally will go looking for a feature gate on a 1.33 cluster, not find one, and either burn an afternoon or conclude the prerequisite is unmet. Two sentences here, and Modules 02 and 03 finally say the same thing.

loc: Lesson05_Restores_and_Day_to_Day_Administration.html · Who can do what · 04 · "Where the boundaries land in practice", first paragraph
orig: Two scoping facts are worth carrying into your first design. Cluster-scoped restore points sit outside the namespace model: access to a ClusterRestorePoint is reserved for users with Veeam Kasten administrative privileges through Kubernetes RBAC, because the resources are cluster-scoped [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.718]. And the direction of travel is worth planning for rather than resisting — the documented guidance is to consider implementing multi-tenancy and turning Veeam Kasten into a backup-as-a-service model rather than restricting its usage to a select group of trusted users, which enables user management based on the principle of least privileges while also supporting self-service [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1092].
prop: Two scoping facts are worth carrying into your first design. Cluster-scoped restore points sit outside the namespace model: access to a ClusterRestorePoint is typically reserved for users with Veeam Kasten administrative privileges through Kubernetes RBAC, because the resources are cluster-scoped [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.718] — the guide's hedge is worth keeping, because nothing stops a cluster administrator writing a ClusterRole that grants them more widely, so verify the bindings on your own cluster rather than assuming the default. And the direction of travel is worth planning for rather than resisting — the documented guidance is to consider implementing multi-tenancy and turning Veeam Kasten into a backup-as-a-service model rather than restricting its usage to a select group of trusted users, which enables user management based on the principle of least privileges while also supporting self-service [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1092].
why: Drops a hedge the source deliberately carries. Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.718 reads "Access to ClusterRestorePoint is *typically* reserved for users with Veeam Kasten administrative privileges through Kubernetes RBAC since the resources are cluster-scoped" — a description of the default, not a guarantee the product enforces. The course states it as a rule. On a real cluster it is a ClusterRole away from being false, and this is precisely the sentence a backup owner would quote in an audit answer about who can reach cluster-scoped restore points. Restoring "typically" and adding the verification instruction costs half a line and keeps the claim defensible.
